## Cross-examination of the five answers

**Strongest falsifiable claim on the bench:** the claim that a below-average rating plus growing profit implies an underpriced business - falsifiable at the 2026-10-22 results date against the guided 6,100 million dollars of revenue.

**Blind spots, named:** (1) Every answer leans on one quarter's growth; nobody asked whether the comparative quarter was depressed. (2) The two cancellations in the order backlog passage are quoted by the cautious answers but sized by none. (3) Nobody priced the cash: with a one-month bill at 4.35 percent, the pack's own free-cash-flow yield reading (0.02 as a plain ratio, about 8 percent annualized on the derivation shown) is the whole argument, and only one answer touched it.

**What all five missed:** the events check says nothing is scheduled before results - so the record supports a patient entry plan rather than urgency; none of the five said so.

Writing rules: all five answers explained their case terms; no unexplained acronym found.
synopsis: Five answers, one record, no factual conflict. The bench splits on emphasis, not facts: the case for owning leans on profit growth of 12 percent and a rating below the five-year average; the cautious answers lean on the order backlog's two cancellations and a price that has already recovered most of its range. The sharpest testable claim is that the below-average rating is unearned pessimism; it is scored against guided revenue of 6,100 million dollars at the 2026-10-22 results date. The one number every answer respects: quarterly free cash flow of 1,000 million dollars, derived inside the record with its arithmetic shown. Nothing in the record forces urgency before the results date.
